(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States

No. 25-5343
KENDRICK JARRELL BEAIRD, PETITIONER
v.
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE FIFTH CIRCUIT

REPLY BRIEF FOR THE UNITED STATES

As the government’s  opening brief explains (Br. 14 -
28), this is a straightforward case.  In Stinson v. United
States, 508 U.S. 36 (1993), this Court held that the “measure” of deference to be afforded to the Sentencing Commission’s commentary to its sentencing guidelines  is the
same as the measure  afforded to “an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations” under Bowles v. Seminole
Rock & Sand Co., 325 U.S. 410 (1945).   Stinson, 508 U.S.
at 45.  In Kisor v. Wilkie, 588 U.S. 558 (2019),  the Court
“reinforc[ed] some of the limits inherent in”  that measure of deference .  Id. at 574.  The plain result of adding
those two decisions together is that th e limits “inherent
in” Seminole Rock deference apply to guidelines commentary as well.  And while th ose limits will frequently
be satisfied in that context, the court of appeals erred in
ignoring them altogether , necessitating vacatur and remand of the decision below.

2

Neither petitioner nor the Court -appointed amicus
curiae (amicus) can refute the simple logic that resolves
this case.  Indeed, until his opening merits brief in this
Court, petitioner agreed with it, and it remains the core
of his backup argument.  See Pet. Br. 36 -42.  His new
principal argument —that commentary in fact warrants
no deference , see id. at  14-34, 42 -45—is unpreserved ,
outside the question presented, and of no consistent
benefit to criminal defendants, some of whom  seek the
benefit of commentary that would lower their guidelines
ranges.  Petitioner’s argument is also unsound on the
merits, as he cannot justify overruling Stinson’s statutory-interpretation holding.  Far from repudiating Stinson, Congress’s actions have been consistent with it.  Indeed, just last year, Congress reviewed and permitted
an update to Sentencing Guidelines § 1B1.7 , which reiterated the longstanding instruction that commentary
“may interpret [a] guideline or explain how it is to be
applied” and that “[f]ailure to follow such commentary
could constitute an incorrect application of the guidelines, subjecting the sentence to possible re versal on appeal.”  Sentencing Guidelines App. C (Vol. IV),  Amend.
836, at 358 (Nov. 1, 2025).
At the opposite extreme, amicus can defend the approach below—which would permit deference to commentary even if the guideline text is unambiguous —
only by reconceiving Stinson, the statutes on which it
relies, and the Commission’s own understanding of its
Guidelines Manual.  In particular, a micus posits that
Congress, this Court, and the Commission have all been
mistaken in the understanding that “commentary” is
one of “three varieties” of text in the Guidelines Manual .
Stinson, 508 U.S. at 41  (emphasis added) .  As amicus
would have it, “commentary” is actually a  “policy state-

3

ment” (Br. 18-24)—or even part of an actual “guideline”
(Br. 39 -47).  But w hile the Commission might well have
been able to enact what is now commentary , say, as a
policy statement instead , that is not what it did.  Accordingly, commentary promotes the goal of sentencing uniformity not through reflexive adherence, but through
deference t o the Commission’s  formal expert interpretations of guidelines ambiguity under Kisor.
A. Guidelines Commentary Warrant s Seminole Rock Deference
1. Stinson  appropriately applies the Seminole Rock approach to guidelines commentary
As the government ’s opening brief explains (Br. 16-
17, 19 -21), Stinson appropriately determined  that the
“measure” of deference given to an agency’s interpretations of its regulations  under Seminole Rock should also
supply the “standard” for deciding “whether particular
interpretive or explanatory commentary is binding .”
508 U.S. at 43 , 45 .  I n making that determination, the
Court drew an “analogy ,” though a “not precise” one,
between guidelines commentary and  an executive
agency’s interpretation of its own regulations , and
found that  replicating the Seminole Rock “measure of
controlling authority” from th e latter context “is consistent with the role the Sentencing Reform Act contemplates for the Sentencing Commission.”  Id. at 44 -
45.
In that statute, “Congress necessarily contemplated
that the Commission would periodically review the work
of the courts, and would make whatever clarifying revisions to the Guidelines conflicting judicial decisions might
suggest. ”  Stinson, 508 U.S. at 46 (quoting Braxton  v.
United States , 500 U.S. 344, 348 (1991) ); see 28 U.S.C.

4

994(o).  And one “method open to the Commission” for
doing so “is amendment of the commentary, if the
guideline [s] which the commentary interprets will bear
the construction.”  Stinson, 508 U.S. at 46.
From their very first iteration through the present
day, commentary has been a central feature of the Guidelines Manual—and one that Congress and this Court have
acknowledged and recognized .  See Stinson, 508 U.S. at
41; see also, e.g., United States  v. Rivera, 76 F.4th 1085,
1090 (8th Cir. 2023)  (citing post -Stinson statutes addressing commentary), cert. denied, 144 S. Ct. 861 (2024).
Like other syntheses of guiding principles, such as the
Restatements  of the Law  or the Model Penal Code, the
Guidelines Manual utilizes below -the-line commentary
—principally in the form of “Application Notes” —to authoritatively clarify the meaning of the more  concise
textual provisions.  See  e.g., Pugin v. Garland, 599 U.S.
600, 606 (2023) (relying on comment to the Model Penal
Code); Universal Health  Servs., Inc.  v. United States ,
579 U.S. 176, 188 n.3, 190 n.4 (2016) (relying on commentary to Second Restatements of Contracts and Torts) .
As the Restatement s, Model Penal Code, and guidelines all reflect, it would be quite difficult as a practical
matter for a comprehensive guide for practitioners to
address every possible circumstance in the above -theline text.  “The list of potentially relevant features of
criminal behavior is long; the fact that they can occur in
multiple combinations means that the list of possible
permutations of factors is virtually endless.”  Sentencing Guidelines, Ch. 1, Pt. A.3 (1987).  Historically , critical guidelines, such as the relevant -conduct guideline
and the guidelines for grouping multiple charges into a
single sentencing recommendation —all of which are
central to the guidelines’ “  ‘real offense ’ sentencing ”

5

approach , id. Ch. 1, Pt. A.4(a) —come with pages of commentary.   See id. §§ 1B1.3, 3D1.1-3D1.5 (2025).
Folding all of that into text, without creating unwarranted cross -inferences and negative inferences, all
while maintaining the Manual’s utility for practitioners,
would be a daunting task .  The Commission has accordingly resolved some of the many complexities inherent
in applying the guidelines text to real -world sentencing
matters through plain-English expository commentary
that typically undergoes public notice -and-comment
and congressional review.  See U.S. Sent. Comm’n R.
4.1, 4.3 ; cf. Securities & Exchange Comm’n  v. Chenery
Corp., 332 U.S. 194, 203 (1947) (noting that a “problem
may be so specialized and varying in nature as to be impossible of capture within the boundaries of a general
rule,” such that “the agency must retain power to deal
with the problems on a case -to-case basis if the administrative process is to be effective”) .  And it has memorialized that practice in the actual text of Sentencing
Guidelines  § 1B1.7, which Congress has reviewed multiple times  and which specifies that  an interpretation of
a guideline can be “incorrect” for “[f]ailure to follow”
commentary that “interpret [s]” or “explain [s]” the
guideline.  Sentencing Guidelines  §§ 1B1.7 (1987, 2025).
2. Petitioner’s request  to overrule Stinson  is misconceived
a. Petitioner’s claim of no deference is not within the
proper scope of this Court’s review
In the courts below, petitioner’s sole Stinson-related
contention  was that  the application of Seminole Rock
deference to guidelines commentary should incorporate
the limits explicated in Kisor.  See U.S. Br. 9 -11; see
also Pet. 6 (describing briefing on appeal  as contending

6

that “ Kisor * * * cabined the level of deference” owed
under Seminole Rock  and thus “overruled [ Stinson] to
the extent  that [ Stinson] requires courts to adhere to
the Commentary unless it actively conflicts with the
text of the Guideline ”) (emphasis added).  And the petition for a writ of certiorari  contended  only that “Kisor
* * * cast[] doubt on Stinson” by “emphasiz[ing] important limitations in Seminole Rock .”  Pet. 16; see Pet.
15-17.
The second question presented thus asked  only
“[w]hether Stinson v.  United States  still accurately
state [sic] the level of deference due to the Commentary
of the Federal Sentencing Guidelines ,” Pet. i (emphasis
added), not whether deference should be discarded altogether.  The Court’s s light rewording of the question
presented, which replaced  “level of deference” with
“rule for the deference ,” 2026 WL 1052007  (emphasis
added), allowed the question to more precisely track  the
difference between the decision below and Kisor, whose
limits concern both the “level” of deference (how much
deference has accorded) and the conditions that must be
satisfied for any deference to apply.  See, e.g., Kisor,
588 U.S. at 577 ( limiting deference to interpretations
that are “actually made by the agency”) .
Nonetheless, petitioner’s principal contention  in his
opening merits brief in this Court —to which the government has not previously had an opportunity to
respond —is that “no deference ” at all is warranted to
guidelines commentary.   Pet. Br. 14 (capitalization
omitted); see id. at 14 -34.  That argument is neither
properly preserved nor within the question presented .
It would accordingly be appropriate for the Court to decline to entertain it, and to limit its review to the issues
presented in the lower courts and at the certiorari stage.

7

b. Petitioner provides no sufficient justification for
overruling Stinson
Even if petitioner’s request to overrule Stinson were
properly before the Court, it should be rejected.  “Overruling precedent is never a small matter.”  Kisor, 588
U.S. at 586 (quoting Kimble v. Marvel Entm’t, LLC, 576
U.S. 446, 455 (2015)).  “[D]eference decisions” like Stinson “are ‘balls tossed into Congress’s court, for acceptance or not as that branch elects. ’ ”  Id. at 587 -588
(quoting Kimble, 576 U.S. at 456) .  And because “Congress remains free to alter what [the Court has] done ,”
adherence to precedent has  “special force .”  Halliburton Co.  v. Erica P. John Fund, Inc. , 573 U.S. 258, 274
(2014) (citation omitted).  Here, in the 33 years since
Stinson “ ‘tossed’ ” its deference ball to Congress to accept or reject,  “Congress  has chosen acceptance ,” Kisor, 588 U.S. at 587 -588 (citation omitted) —if not outright endorsement.
i. As noted above, Congress has recently reviewed
Sentencing Guidelines § 1B1.7, titled “Significance of
Commentary,” which makes clear that it may be reversible error to apply the guidelines in a manner contrary to the commentary.  See Sentencing Guidelines
§ 1B1.7.  Congress has  also reviewed numerous guidelines whose interpretation may turn on deference to
commentary and allowed them to become effective.
Since 1997, the Commission has , by rule,  “endeavor [ed]
to include amendments to  * * * commentary in any submission of guideline amendments to Congress ,” U.S.
Sent. Comm’n R. 4.1 , thereby apprising Congress of the
role that commentary may play in guidelines’ application.
Congress has even gone so far as to direct the Commission to reconsider interpretive commentary in light

8

of policy concerns.  See Stop Counterfeiting in Manufactured Goods Act,  Pub. L. No. 109 -181, § 1(c)(3), 120
Stat. 28 7 (2006) (requiring reconsideration of “ the definition of ‘infringement amount’ set forth in application
note 2 of section 2B5.3”) ; Artists’ Rights and Theft Prevention Act of 2005,  Pub. L. No. 109-9, Tit. I, § 105(c)(3),
119 Stat. 223 (requiring reconsideration of “scope of ‘uploading’ set forth in application note 3 of section 2B5.3”) .
That makes little sense unless the commentary can, indeed, illuminate  the meaning of an ambiguous  guideline
—precisely what Stinson says.  See, e.g., Ryan v. Gonzales, 568 U.S. 57, 66 (2013) ( “We normally assume that,
when Congress enacts statutes, it is aware of relevant
judicial precedent.”) (citation omitted).
ii. Petitioner cannot carry his “considerable burden,” CBOCS W ., Inc. v. Humphries , 553 U.S. 442, 451
(2008), to provide a “ ‘special justification’ —something
more than ‘an argument that the precedent was wrong -
ly decided ’ ”—that would  justify overruling Stinson.
Kisor, 588 U.S. at 587 (quoting Halliburton , 573 U.S. at
266); see Amicus Br. 47-51.  Indeed, petitioner primarily
tries to avoid taking on that burden , asserting  that
“[t]his Court need not consider the stare decisis  factors” to overrule Stinson, on the theory that Loper
Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo , 603 U.S. 369 (2024),
already shows that Stinson is incorrect and that Kisor
is “an ‘aber ration.’  ”  Pet. Br. 42 -43 (citation omitted);
see e.g., id. at 14, 18, 23.   That theory is unsound.
Loper Bright  overruled deference to agency interpretations of statutes  under Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984),
on the ground that such deference “cannot be squared
with the [Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C.
551 et seq., 701 et seq.],” which “makes clear that agency

9

interpretations of statutes ” are “not entitled to deference.”  Loper Bright , 603 U.S. at 392, 396  (emphasis
omitted).  That overruled Chevron doctrine has no meaningful bearing on Stinson, which expressly rejected an
analogy between Chevron deference to agencies’ statutory interpretations and deference to guidelines commentary as “inapposite.”   Stinson, 508 U.S. at 44.
Whereas Chevron deference rested on a “presumption” that Congress delegated authority to an agency to
“resolve[]” “ambiguity in a statute” written by Congress,
Loper Bright , 603 U.S. at 398  (citation omitted) , the
Commission’s commentary  “explains the guidelines”
that the Commission itself enacts, Stinson, 508 U.S. at
44.  And because “ [c]ommentary, unlike a legislative
rule, is not the product of delegated authority for rulemaking,” t he closest analogue for guidelines commentary was not Chevron deference, but the Seminole Rock
deference afforded to “an agency’s interpretation of its
own legislative rule.”  Ibid.
While Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference,
Kisor “uph[e]ld” Seminole Rock deferenc e.  Kisor, 588
U.S. at 563 .  And when it did so, a ll five of the six Justices then on the Court who would later  join the majority in Loper Bright  made clear  that “[i]ssues surrounding judicial deference to agency interpretations of their
own regulations  are distinct from those raised in connection with judicial deference to agency interpretations of statutes enacted by Congress.”  Id. at 591 (Roberts, C.J., concurring in part); id. at 633 (Kavanaugh, J.,
joined by Alito, J., concurring in the judgment) (agreeing with the Chief Justice); see id. at 628 n.114 (Gorsuch, J., joined by Thomas and Kavanaugh, JJ., concurring in the judgment) (similarly stating that “it would
be a mistake to suppose that Auer”—another name for

10

the Seminole Rock  doctrine —“is in any way a ‘logical
corollary to Chevron’ ”) (citation omitted).
Loper Bright itself favorably cites Kisor multiple
times.  See Loper Bright , 603 U.S. at 392 -393, 401.  And
deference to guidelines commentary would be a particularly inapt context for extending Loper Bright, because
the APA provision that is central to Loper Bright ’s
holding—5 U.S.C. 706 (see, e.g., Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at
390-394, 398)—does not apply to the guidelines.  See 28
U.S.C. 994(x) (separately applying different APA provision); United States  v. Maiello, 805 F.3d 992, 998 (11th
Cir. 2015) ( agreeing with the Third, Eighth, Ninth, and
D.C. Circuits “that the Commission is not an ‘agency’
subject to the requirements of the APA”); S. Rep. No.
225, 98th Cong., 1st Sess. 180 -181 & n.420 (1983) .
Nor, for that matter, did  Stinson even apply Seminole Rock deference as such.  Instead, as noted above,
Stinson simply replicated  the “standard ” and “measure” for deference in Seminole Rock , based on an “analogy” between the Commission’s interpretation of its
own guideline and “an agency’s interpretation of its own
legislative rule” —an analogy that it recognized was
“not precise.”   Stinson, 508 U.S. at 43-45.  And while the
analogy may be stronger today than it was when Stinson was decided, see U.S. Br. 20-21, Loper Bright’s APA-
focused reasoning  in no way undermines Stinson’s determination that the Seminole Rock approach  is “ consistent with the role the Sentencing Reform  Act contemplates for the Sentencing Commission ,” 508 U.S. at
45.
c. Petitioner’s criticisms of Stinson lack merit
To the extent that petitioner effectivel y contends
(Br. 15-21) that Stinson was simply wrong as an original
matter in finding Seminole Rock deference to be con-

11

sistent with the governing statutes , that contention provides no “special justification ,” Kisor, 5 88 U.S. at 587
(citation omitted), for overruling Stinson.  The contention is also mistaken.
Petitioner observes (Br. 14 -17) that the sentencing
statutes require a sentencing court to consider the “kinds
of sentence” and “sentencing range” recommended in the
guidelines, 18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(4), and “correctly” ascertain
the advisory sentencing range, Gall v. United States ,
552 U.S. 38, 49 (2007 ).  But as the Court necessarily recognized in Stinson, those requirements are consistent
with deferring to the Commission’s commentary when
interpreting a guideline.  See 508 U.S. at 4 5-46 (considering Commission’s role under Sentencing Reform Act).
Indeed, the guidelines themselves direct courts to pay
heed to the commentary .  See Sentencing Guidelines
§ 1B1.7.  Petitioner’s reliance (Br. 17-18) on decisions
reflecting that courts are responsible for evaluating
whether the Commission’s instructions are consistent
with the relevant  statute sheds no meaningful light on
commentary’s role in interpreting ambiguous guidelines.
Petitioner is similarly mistaken in his claim (Br. 20)
that Seminole Rock deference  is an “end-run” around
the procedures for promulgating and amending guidelines.  Even putting aside the Commission’s practice
of subjecting commentary to the same majority -vote,
notice-and-comment, and congressional -review procedures as guidelines,  see U.S. Sent. Comm’n R. 4.1, 4.3 ,
petitioner errs in assuming that commentary can amend
the guidelines sub silentio.  C ommentary is not itself a
guideline ; instead, it is dependent upon, and subsidiary
to, the guidelines text.  See Stinson, 508 U.S. at 46 (requiring that “the guideline which the commentary interprets will bear the construction ”); see also Kisor, 588

12

U.S. at 574-576 (emphasizing that Seminole Rock deference is limited to “genuinely ambiguous” rules) .  As
the Court has explained, Seminole Rock deference
“does not, and indeed could not,  go” so “far” as to “  ‘permit the agency, under the guise of interpreting a regulation, to create de facto a new regulation.’  ”  Kisor, 588
U.S. at 575 (citation omitted).
Much less does deference to the Commission’s commentary usurp Congress’ authority to “define crimes
and fix punishments,” Pet. Br. 26 (citation omitted) , or
raise any other possible “constitutional concerns,” id. at
21.  This Court has squarely rejected the claim that the
promulgation even of binding  sentencing guidelines is
an impermissible  “exercise *  * * [of ] legislative authority” to “make[] *  * * sentencing policy .”  Mistretta  v.
United States , 488 U.S. 361, 3 83 (1989); see id. at 384-
397.  It follows a fortiori that deference to commentary
interpreting nonbinding  guidelines —which the Commission does not enforce, and which have less legal force
than binding ones , see U.S. Br. 21—is likewise constitutionally permissible .  Cf. Amicus Br. 37.
B. Kisor Makes Clear That Seminole Rock Deference Cannot Overcome Unambiguous Regulatory Text
Because the “limits” emphasized in Kisor are “inherent in” Seminole Rock deference , Kisor, 588 U.S. at 574,
they are necessarily  inherent in Stinson’s adoption of
that same “measure of controlling authority” as “the
standard that governs the decision whether particular
interpretive or explanatory commentary is binding ,”
Stinson, 508 U.S. at 43, 45.  As Kisor makes clear, even
the “class ic formulation” of Seminole Rock deference
that appears in Stinson—a shorthand reference to
whether  an agency’s construction is “  ‘plainly erroneous
or inconsistent with the regulation ’ ”—does not permit

13

deference in the absence of “genuine ambiguity” and
the other prerequisites  identified in Kisor.  588 U.S. at
574-575 (citation omitted) ; see id. at 57 4-579; see also
U.S. Br. 18-19.  Amicus errs in nonetheless  urging a “reflexive, ” Kisor, 588 U.S. at 574  (citation omitted), form
of deference that would permit deference to commentary even when a guideline is unambiguous.
1. Rather than try to meaningfully defend  Stinson
on its own terms, amicus instead attempts to reconceptualize both that decision and the entire legal and practical framework that underlies it .  Specifically, he contends (Br. 18 -28) that the Commission’s “commentary”
actually consists of “policy statement [s]” that Congress
has “expressly ” authorized under 28 U.S.C. 994(a)(2),
and should therefore be treated as an “authoritative
guide to the meaning of the applicable Guideline” under
this Court’s decision in Williams  v. United States , 503
U.S. 193 , 201 (1992).  But neither Congress, this Court,
nor the Commission itself have understood commentary
to be policy statements.
Amicus observes  that Section 994(a)(2) authorizes
the Commission “to promulgate ‘general policy statements regarding application of the guidelines.’  ”  Br. 18
(quoting 28 U.S.C. 994(a)(2)).  And it may well be the
case that the Commission could have promulgated commentary, or something similar, under that authority.
But just because policy statements may “regard[] application of the guidelines,” 28 U.S.C. 99 4(a)(2), does not
mean that everything that regards application of the
guidelines  is a policy statement.  Cf. United States Dep ’t
of Justice  v. Tax Analysts , 492 U.S. 136, 154 (1989)  (“If
Congress had intended to enact the converse proposition * * * it was free to do so .”).  Just as a uthorizing the
production of cars that are red does not make every red

14

object a car , Section 994(a)(2) does not make commentary into policy statements.
Stinson instead explained  that there are “ three varieties” of text in the Guidelines Manual —“guideline,”
“policy state ment,” and “commentary” —each of which
Congress distinctly addressed by name in the Sentencing Reform Act.  508 U.S. at 41  (emphasis added) .  Stinson accordingly treated the issue of the deference due
to commentary as distinct from the issue of the deference due to a policy statement.  The Court  found that
its “holding in Williams ,” which required setting aside
a sentence  under 18 U.S.C. 3742(f  )(1) for a prejudicial
failure to follow a policy statement, “applie [d] with
equal force to the commentary before us here.”  Stinson, 508 U.S.  at 43; see id. at 42  (citing Williams , 503
U.S. at 201, 203).  It immediately cautioned, however,
that “[i]t does not follow that commentary is binding in
all instances.”  Id. at 43.  The Court  then proceeded
through several pages of analysis of “the standard that
governs the decision whether particular interpretive or
explanatory commen tary.”  Ibid.; see id. at 43-47.  All of
that analysis would have been unnecessary if the commentary were itself a policy statement.
Congress has likewise treated commentary as distinct from policy statements.  The (now -invalidated) 18
U.S.C. 3553(b) (1) refers to “sentencing guidelines, policy statements, and official commentary of the Sentencing Commission,” 18 U.S.C. 3553(b)(1)  (emphasis
added), indicating that they are, in fact, three distinct
things.  See , e.g., Parker Drilling Mgmt. Servs. , Ltd. v.
Newton, 587 U.S. 601, 611 (2019) (recognizing the “ ‘cardinal principle ’ of interpretation that courts ‘must give
effect, if possible, to every clause and word of a statute.’ ”) (quoting Loughrin v. United States , 573 U.S.

15

351, 358 (2014)).  Nor can it reasonably be supposed that
when C ongress has directed changes to, or reconsideration of, particular application notes , see p. 8, supra, it
has failed to recognize that those application notes appear under the heading of “Commentary.”  See Sentencing Guidelines § 2B5.3, comment.  (nn.2-3) (2004);
id. § 3E1.1, comment. (n. 6) (2002); id. § 4B1.5, comment .
(n.4) (2005).
The classification of application notes as commentary is also, in itself, a dispositive reason to reject petitioner’s recharacterization of those application notes as
policy statements.  The label attached by the Commission reflects that the Commission itself is not promulgating th e application notes pursuant to its authority to
promulgate policy statements.  Although the Commission’s rules prescribe similar procedures for policy statements and commentary, see Amicus Br. 18-20, the separate denomination of each shows that the Commission —
like Congress and this Court —views them as different
things.  See U.S. Sent. Comm’n R. 4.1, 4.3  (Commission
rules referring  to “promulgat [ing]” both “policy statements and commentary ”) (emphasis added).
Sentencing Guidelines § 1B1.7, in addressing the
“Significance of Commentary,” has  likewise  (in both its
text and commentary) treated policy statements and
commentary as distinct.  See Sentencing Guidelines
§ 1B1.7 (1987) (using both terms); id. § 1B1.7 comment.
(suggesting only that certain commentary would “have
the force of policy statements”); Sentencing Guidelines
§ 1B1.7 comment. (2025) (same).   The Commission’s actions to promulgate  “commentary ,” ibid., cannot be reasonably understood to have actually been actions to
promulgate “policy statements,” ibid.—let alone retroactively reclassified as such.   Cf. Garland v. Ming Dai ,

16

593 U.S. 357, 369 (2021) (noting the “traditional administrative law principle []” that  “judges generally must
assess the lawfulness of an  agency’s action in light of the
explanations the  agency offered for it rather than any
ex post rationales  a court can devise ”).
Similar conceptual errors undermine amicus’s alternative theory (Br. 39-46) that “commentary” is actually
a “guideline” provision to which the Commission has
voluntarily assigned less weight.  Amicus acknowledges
(Br. 40)  that accepting that theory would be a “reframing” that “would not track Stinson’s reasoning.”  The
theory also rests on an incurable circularity.   In a micus’s view (e.g., Br. 39), the reason why portions of a
guideline denominated as commentary would be treated
differently from the text is because the commentary to
Sentencing Guidelines § 1B1.7 about the weight of
guidelines commentary references Stinson.  In other
words, amicus’s argument relies on a reference in commentary  to a decision adopted at a time when the Sentencing Guidelines § 1B1.7 contained different  commentary, see Stinson, 508 U.S. at 46, and whose reasoning
he admits that he does not defend , Amicus Br. 40.  Such
a conceptual ouroboros cannot provide a foundation for
his approach.
2. Amicus separate ly contends  (Br. 3 0-32) that application of Kisor to Stinson would conflict with Loper
Bright.  But like petitioner, amicus errs in attempting
to transpose Loper Bright ’s reasoning about Chevron
into the context of Seminole Rock deference as incorporated by Stinson.  In particular, Loper Bright ’s reasoning does not undermine recognizing that Kisor’s “genuine ambiguity” limit on Seminole Rock deference, Kisor, 588 U.S. at 57 5, is similarly “inherent in” Stinson’s
incorporation of that approach, id. at 574.

17

Amicus notes that Chevron deference to an agency’s
interpretation of a congressional statute, which the
Court discarded in Loper Bright , “rested on a presumption that Congress, when it left ambiguity in a statute
meant for implementation by an agency, understood
that the ambiguity would be resolved, first and foremost, by the agency.”  Amicus Br. 30 (quoting Loper
Bright, 603 U.S. at 398).  And he additionally notes that
Loper Bright set aside Chevron deference, in part, because it found Chevron’s “ambiguity” trigger to be too
“impressionistic and malleable” to “  ‘stand as an ever yday test for allocating ’ interpretive authority between
courts and agencies. ”  Loper Bright , 603 U.S. at 408 (citation omitted) ; see Amicus Br. 31.  But f ar from foreclosing a determination of ambiguity from ever forming
a part of statutory interpretation, Loper Bright simply
rejected ambiguity as a basis for an approach that
would require a court to “give up on its ‘interpretive
work’ ” and simply “allow the Executive Branch to displace” the court’s own interpretation of the Legislative
Branch’s enactments.  Loper Bright , 603 U.S. at 409.
The Seminole Rock approach under Stinson, as informed by Kisor, requires no such thing.
As a threshold matter, a s noted above (see p. 9, supra), Stinson expressly rejected  an analogy  between
Chevron deference (the subject in Loper Bright ) and
deference to guidelines commentary .  And as discussed
above (see ibid.), the Loper Bright  presumption that
amicus highlights —under which Congress was presumed to delegate authority to interpret Congress’s  enactments to third-party executive agencies (which could
switch positions over time) , see Loper Bright , 603 U.S.
at 398 -406—plays no role in Seminole Rock deference
under Stinson.  As the Court explained in Stinson, the

18

Seminole Rock approach of deferring to  an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations  “is consistent with
the role the Sentencing Reform Act contemplates for
the Sentencing Commission,” which, “after all,  drafts
the guidelines as well as the commentary interpreting
them.”  Stinson, 508 U.S. at 45 (emphasis added) .
Nor did Loper Bright cast general doubt on statutory-
interpretation doctrines that turn on ambiguity.  To the
contrary, while the Court acknowledged  that the dissent had identified several such doctrines , such as the
“canon of constitutional avoidance,” Loper Bright , 603
U.S. at 474 (Kagan, J., dissenting) , the Court did not
deny either their viability or workability.   See id. at 409
(majority opinion) .  And the “genuine ambiguity” analysis under Kisor, which limits deference to circumstances in which the traditional tools of statutory analysis leave more than “one reasonable construction of a
regulation ,” Kisor, 588 U.S. at 575 , functions much like
the ambiguity prerequisite for constitutional avoidance,
which “comes into play only when, after the application
of ordinary textual analysis, [a] statute is found to be
susceptible of more than one construction ,” Jennings  v.
Rodriguez , 583 U.S. 281, 2 96 (2018)  (citation omitted) .
C. Deference To Guidelines Commentary Will Frequently
Satisfy The Limits Explicated in Kisor
As the government’s opening brief explains (Br. 22-
28), even under the limits of Seminole Rock deference
emphasized in Kisor, deference to guidelines commentary will frequently be warranted.  The commentary
represent s the Commission’s formal, considered judgments on guidelines application ( id. at 26); it embodies
the Commission’s statutorily -mandated expertise on
such matters  (id. at 26-27); and its assistance to courts
struggling with the genuine ambiguity that is inevitable

19

in generalized nationwide sentencing guidelines is typically reasonable ( id. at 22-25).  Deference under that
approach does not inherently favor any particular outcome.  As illustrated in Stinson, which itself involved
commentary that suggested a lower sentencing range,
see 508 U.S. at 38 -39, commentary does not always favor harsher sentencing outcomes —it can go either way.
Petitioner, however, urges this Court, if it accepts his
original argument that Stinson should be understood in
light of Kisor, to limit any deference to commentary that
would lower a defendant’s guidelines range, while categorially rejecting deference to  commentary that would
suggest a higher advisory guidelines range.  See Pet. Br.
40-41.  But his sole basis for that one -sided approach —
the rule of lenity —does not provide it with any support.
1. “[M]uch like the vagueness doctrine,” the rule of
lenity is “founded on” two principles: (1) that “ ‘the power
of punishment is vested in the legislative, not in the judicial department ’ ” and (2) that individuals are entitled
to “fair notice of the law .”  United States  v. Davis, 588
U.S. 445, 464 -465 (2019) (quoting United States  v. Wiltberger, 18 U.S. (5 Wheat.) 76, 95 (1820) (Marshall, C.J.));
accord United States  v. Bass, 404 U.S. 336, 348 (1971)
(stating that lenity is “founded on [those] two policies”).
Accordingly, t he logic underlying the Court’s rejection
of separation-of-powers and vagueness challenges to the
guidelines  compels the conclusion that the rule of lenity
does not apply in the context of deference to guidelines
commentary.   See Beckles v. United States , 580 U.S.
256, 26 2-267 (2017)  (vagueness); Mistretta , 488 U.S. at
384-397 (separation of powers).
As discussed above  (see p. 12, supra), deference to
guidelines commentary does not implicate the principle
that “legislatures and not courts should define criminal

20

activity ,” Bass, 404 U.S. at 348 .  See Mistretta , 488 U.S.
at 396 .  This Court has similarly made clear that “[t]he
advisory Guidelines  also do not implicate” concerns
about “ ‘fair notice. ’ ”  Beckles, 580 U.S. at 262, 265 (citation omitted).  The guidelines  “do not regulate the public by prohibiting any conduct or by ‘establishing minimum and maximum penalties for any crime.’  ”  Id. at 266
(citation and brackets omitted).  Those functions are instead carried out  exclusively by the underlying criminal
statutes in a case.  The now-advisory guidelines play the
distinctly subsidiary role of “advis[ing] sentencing
courts how to exercise their discretion within the
bounds established by Congress.”   Ibid.  And courts’ exercise of such discretion , so long as it honors the minimum and maximum punishments established by Congress, has never given rise to the concerns underlying
the rule of lenity .  See id. at 267 (discussing the “unfettered discretion” of a sentencing judge to select a sentence within the statutory range).
Petitioner errs in suggesting (Br. 25 -26) that the rule
of lenity should nonetheless apply as a vestige of what
he presumes to be Congress’s  implicit  intent before
United States v. Booker, 543 U.S. 220 (2005) , when the
guidelines were treated as mandatory.  To begin with ,
the more relevant focus is on the Commission’s  intent,
not Congress’s —“[t]he Commission, after all, drafts the
guidelines” whose text might trigger a lenity presumption.  Stinson, 508 U.S. at 45.  Furthermore, the Court’s
assessment of congressional intent in  its pre-Booker decision in Stinson—which made clear that it was addressing the standard for all commentary, see id. at 43-44—
indicates that Congress did not intend for the rule of
lenity to limit deference only to defendant -favorable
commentary.  See id. at 45.

21

Finally, even if Congress had such an unstated intent
at that time, it is far from clear that it woul d retain it
for advisory guidelines.  See Booker, 543 U.S. at 246 (examining what “Congress would have intended” if it
knew that its original design for mandatory guidelines
was constitutionally infirm) (citation omitted).   To the
contrary,  after Booker, Congress has directed the Commission to reconsider interpretive commentary based
on considerations that could suggest commentary that
would favor higher sentencing range s for certain criminal conduct.  See p. 8, supra (discussing 120 Stat. 287
and 199 Stat. 223).  Those statutory directives would
have little effect if such commentary would simply be
ignored.
2. In any event, even if the rule of lenity might otherwise be relevant,  it applies “only when a criminal statute contains a ‘grievous ambiguity or uncertainty’  ” that
leaves a court —even “  ‘after seizing everything from
which [interpretive] aid can be derived ’ ”—unable to
“ ‘make * * * more than a guess as to what Congress intended.’  ”  Ocasio v. United States , 578 U.S. 282, 295 n.8
(2016) (quoting Muscarello  v. United States , 524 U.S.
125, 138 (1998)).  For that reason, “[t]he rule ‘comes into
operation at the end of the process of construing what
Congress has expressed.’  ”  Wooden v. United States, 595
U.S. 360, 37 7 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring) (quoting Callanan  v. United States , 364 U.S. 587, 596 (1961)).
Those limits do not allow it to  be employed to foreclose
Seminole Rock deference under Stinson and Kisor.
Petitioner errs in asserting (Br. 41) that “the rule of
lenity” should “take preceden ce” over deference to the
Commission ’s commentary .  The rule of lenity, like deference und er Kisor, applies “only * * * after consulting
traditional canons of statutory construction.”  Shular v.

22

United States, 589 U.S. 154, 165 (2020) (emphasis added);
see Kisor, 588 U.S. at 575.  And at that point,  no “grievous ambiguity,” United States  v. Castleman , 572 U.S.
157, 173 (2014)  (citation omitted), could exist.  A  court is
not left to “simply guess”  at the meaning of the guideline, ibid. (citation omitted) , when the Commission has
reasonably explained that meaning  in the commentary.
When such commentary is present, it supplies the best
source for ensuring that the guidelines are understood
uniformly by the courts tasked with considering its nationwide guidance.  Stinson soundly “presume[d] that
the interpretations of the guidelines contained in the
commentary represent the most accurate indications of
how the Commission deems that the guidelines should
be applied to be consistent with the Guidelines Manual
as a whole as well as the authorizing statute.”  508 U.S.
at 45 (emphasis added).   No legal, logical, or practical
reason exists for categorically disregarding those explanatory interpretations  whenever they do  not match
a defendant’s preferences .  The proper disposition of
this case is to remand for an evenhanded application of
Kisor—not a lopsided one.
